steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Pins: cannot move, or should not move. This part covers Set one up, stop one. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Setting one up.** You need a long-range piece, a target and a screen on one line, then a threat. [I] In the examples here a quiet pin was undone in one move and the wins came with a threat or a check (not counted). [V] Our bank holds 55 pin-themed Lichess puzzles with a find-the-move task. The first move is by a knight in 20, a bishop in 16, a rook in 9, a queen in 9, a pawn in 1, and gives check in 26.

steps.caption: White to move. A check can clear the line before the pin is set.

line.say: The bishop gives check along the diagonal to the king on g7.
The pawn blocks the check, and it leaves the seventh rank, which clears the line from c7 to the king.
The rook pins the queen to the king along the seventh rank.
The queen may take, because she can slide along the line.
The second rook recaptures with check. White has a queen for a rook.

claims.statement: The engine rates White as clearly better.
After the rook arrives, the queen has three legal moves, all along the rank.
After the rook arrives, it attacks the queen.

steps.caption: White to move. A quiet pin: the rook can join the e-file, but the pin may last only one move.

line.say: The rook pins the bishop and prepares the pawn push.
The king steps off the e-file, so the pin is over.
The bishop simply retreats. White has won nothing.

claims.statement: After the rook move, the bishop on e6 has no legal move.
The engine rates the position as roughly level.

steps.caption: White to move. Not a pin: a fork. One piece attacks two targets, with nothing in front of either.

line.say: The knight attacks the king and the rook at once.
The king must answer the check.

claims.statement: After the jump, the knight attacks the king.
After the jump, the knight attacks the rook.
The jump wins material along the engine line.

steps.caption: White to move. Not a pin: a skewer, the pin the other way round. The valuable piece stands in front and must move, so the piece behind falls.

line.say: The rook checks along the h-file. The king stands in front, the rook behind.
The king must step off the file.
The rook takes what stood behind the king.

claims.statement: After the rook move it attacks the king.
The skewer wins the rook along the engine line.

steps.text: **[H] A guess to argue with.** Players may overrate a pin they have made, because a pin is a picture, and underrate the one-move escape, because an escape takes calculation. This is my guess, not a finding; we have not tested it. For your next five games, note each pin you make and how many moves it lasted.

steps.prompt: Do you agree with the guess, or does it match your own games differently? Say why in a sentence.

steps.text: **Stopping a pin against you.** Before each move, find the enemy long-range pieces and ask what stands on their lines to your king and queen. Dan Heisman (*Looking for Trouble*, as summarised on chess.com and ForwardChess [S]) advises looking for the opponent's strongest forcing replies before you move. A pin is often the quiet reply. If one is coming, the five ways out are best used before it arrives.

steps.title: Same bishop, one pawn different
steps.prompt: Predict first. The same attack on the knight, with one small difference between the positions. Does the white bishop on g5 attack the queen once the knight leaves?
What made the difference between the two positions?

fields.label: The difference:
options: the knight is defended in one and not the other
the pawn on e7 blocks the line to the queen
the bishop on g5 is attacked in one
the queen stands on a different square
fields.answer: the pawn on e7 blocks the line to the queen
